strings.name: Annie Ernaux
strings.role: Writer · Social history within personal memory
strings.summary: Ernaux uses her own experience to examine class, gender and social change, connecting personal memory with collective history in restrained prose. A Man’s Place considers her father and class distance; Happening records an illegal abortion; The Years places a generation’s lives within a changing society. Her work explores the border between literature and sociology. She received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Literature, and her books continue to be translated and adapted.

strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Personal experience as social evidence
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Family, education and women’s bodily experience reveal class distances in writing that combines autobiography and social observation.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Collective memory in The Years
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Photographs, habits of consumption and public events structure a decades-spanning narrative that expands autobiography’s form.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: English volume Writing, the Other Life appears
strings.timeline.event-01.text: The research website confirmed the English collection of interviews, criticism and previously untranslated texts; the French volume was compiled by an editor.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Attends the Cannes premiere of A Girl’s Story
strings.timeline.event-02.text: She joined director Judith Godrèche for the premiere of the adaptation of her 2016 book, continuing an exchange between literature and film.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Receives the Nobel Prize in Literature
strings.timeline.event-03.text: The Swedish Academy recognized her examination of personal memory and social constraints, broadening attention to her autobiographical work.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Publishes A Girl’s Story
strings.timeline.event-04.text: She returned to her experiences in 1958 to examine desire, shame and the effects of group norms on a young woman’s identity.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Publishes The Years
strings.timeline.event-05.text: Personal memory, images and social change form a narrative spanning decades, exploring autobiography beyond a single speaking self.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Publishes Happening
strings.timeline.event-06.text: Revisiting her 1963–64 illegal abortion, she connected bodily memory with law, class and the silences of the period.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: A Man’s Place wins the Prix Renaudot
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Her 1983 account of her father received the prize, using spare language to explore familial closeness alongside class distance.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Debuts with Cleaned Out
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Her first published book connected educational mobility and women’s bodily experience, establishing concerns she continued to develop.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Born in Normandy
strings.timeline.event-09.text: Born in Lillebonne and raised in Yvetot, where her parents ran a café and grocery shop; she later studied literature in Rouen.
